text: I had gone to the desert that summer because I no longer trusted the version of myself that lived in the city, the one who answered the telephone and made the appointments and behaved, in every visible particular, as if the center would hold. It did not hold, of course; it had not held for some time, and I think I knew that even as I packed the car, even as I drove east into a light so flat and merciless that it seemed less like weather than like a verdict. I was thirty-one years old. I tell you this not because it matters but because it is the kind of fact I kept reaching for, in those months, the way you reach for a railing in the dark.

The house had been sold and the furniture was gone and what remained was the particular silence of rooms that have stopped expecting anyone. I walked through them slowly, noting the pale rectangles on the walls where the pictures had hung, the dust that had already begun its patient work. We tell ourselves that grief has stages, that it moves and resolves, that one morning we will wake and find it finished. This is a story we tell because the alternative is unbearable, and because we are, all of us, addicted to the consolations of narrative.

It is easy to see the beginnings of things and harder to see the ends. I was living then in a borrowed apartment on a street where the jacaranda dropped its blue flowers onto the cars, and I believed, as one believes at that age, that the arrangements I had made were permanent and that the people I loved were fixed in their places like furniture. They were not. Nothing is. The light changed in October, the way it does in that part of the country, and by the time the rains came I understood that I had been wrong about almost everything, and that the understanding had cost me more than I could yet calculate.

There is a point at which a marriage, or a city, or a year, stops being a thing that is happening to you and becomes instead a thing you have done, and the recognition of that point is among the loneliest a person can experience. I remember the exact hour. I remember the quality of the air. I have learned to distrust my own memory in most matters, to hold my certainties loosely, but about this I am certain, and the certainty is not a comfort. It is simply a fact I carry, cool and smooth, like a stone in a coat pocket.

We drove down to the coast to see the water and instead saw only the fog, which had come in low and stayed, erasing the line between the sea and the sky and giving the whole afternoon the unfinished quality of a sentence trailing off. My daughter slept in the back seat. The radio gave the news in the flat affectless voice they use for catastrophe and for the weather alike, as if there were no difference, as if there had never been a difference, and I thought, not for the first time, that the trick of living was to keep driving anyway.
